title: Trigonometry
why: Trigonometry is one of the most-asked chapters in the IPO maths section: the 2022 paper had direct questions such as the value of $\cos 480^\circ$, the angle opposite the largest side of a triangle with sides $a, \sqrt3a, \sqrt2a$, and the distance between the tops of two poles. Nearly every question reduces to the standard-angle table plus one rule (ASTC, a compound-angle formula, a principal-value range, the cosine rule or $\tan$ = height/distance), so a few hours here pays off across many marks.

lessons.title: 1. Angles, degrees and radians
lessons.body:
### An angle measures turning
Stand facing east and turn anticlockwise until you face east again: that is one full turn $= 360^\circ$. A quarter turn is $90^\circ$ (a right angle), a half turn $180^\circ$ (a straight line). Smaller units: $1^\circ = 60'$ (minutes) and $1' = 60''$ (seconds).
Turning **anticlockwise** is counted as **positive**, turning clockwise as **negative**. Angles can be bigger than $360^\circ$ (more than one full turn), e.g. $480^\circ = 360^\circ + 120^\circ$.

### The radian
Draw a circle of radius $r$. Walk along the edge a distance equal to $r$. The angle this arc makes at the centre is **1 radian**. The whole edge (circumference) is $2\pi r$, i.e. $2\pi$ radii, so a full turn is $2\pi$ radians:
$$2\pi \text{ rad} = 360^\circ \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \pi \text{ rad} = 180^\circ$$
(1 radian $\approx 57.3^\circ$.) When no degree sign is written — $\sin\frac{\pi}{6}$, $\cos 2$ — the angle is in radians.

### Converting
- Degrees → radians: multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$. $\ 150^\circ = 150\times\dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.
- Radians → degrees: replace $\pi$ by $180^\circ$. $\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4} = \dfrac{3\times180^\circ}{4} = 135^\circ$.

| Degrees | $30^\circ$ | $45^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $90^\circ$ | $120^\circ$ | $135^\circ$ | $150^\circ$ | $180^\circ$ | $270^\circ$ | $360^\circ$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Radians | $\frac{\pi}{6}$ | $\frac{\pi}{4}$ | $\frac{\pi}{3}$ | $\frac{\pi}{2}$ | $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ | $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ | $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ | $\pi$ | $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ | $2\pi$ |

### Arc length
If an arc of a circle of radius $r$ subtends angle $\theta$ **in radians** at the centre, its length is
$$l = r\theta$$
**Mini example.** Radius 14 cm, angle $45^\circ = \frac{\pi}{4}$: $l = 14\times\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 14\times\dfrac{22}{7\times4} = 11$ cm. (Always convert degrees to radians first.)

### Bonus: angle between clock hands
The minute hand turns $6^\circ$ per minute; the hour hand $0.5^\circ$ per minute. At $H$ hours $M$ minutes the angle between them is $|30H - 5.5M|$ (if it exceeds $180^\circ$, subtract from $360^\circ$). At 3:40 → $|90 - 220| = 130^\circ$.

> **Recognise it in the exam:** "express in radians", "$\frac{5\pi}{6}$ in degrees", "length of arc", "a wheel turns … find the angle", "angle between the hands of a clock". Tools: $\pi = 180^\circ$, $l = r\theta$.

lessons.title: 2. The six ratios and the standard-angle table
lessons.body:
### Ratios in a right-angled triangle
Take a right-angled triangle and one acute angle $\theta$. Name the sides **as seen from $\theta$**:
- **Perpendicular** $P$ (opposite side) — the side facing $\theta$
- **Base** $B$ (adjacent side) — the side next to $\theta$ (not the hypotenuse)
- **Hypotenuse** $H$ — the longest side, facing the right angle

| Ratio | Definition | Reciprocal |
|---|---|---|
| $\sin\theta$ | $P/H$ | $\csc\theta = H/P$ |
| $\cos\theta$ | $B/H$ | $\sec\theta = H/B$ |
| $\tan\theta$ | $P/B$ | $\cot\theta = B/P$ |

Memory line: "**S**ome **P**eople **H**ave **C**urly **B**rown **H**air **T**hrough **P**roper **B**rushing" → $\sin = \frac{P}{H}$, $\cos = \frac{B}{H}$, $\tan = \frac{P}{B}$. Also $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$.

### Given one ratio, find the rest
**Mini example.** $\sin\theta = \frac35$ ($\theta$ acute). So $P = 3$, $H = 5$, and by Pythagoras $B = \sqrt{25 - 9} = 4$. Then $\cos\theta = \frac45$, $\tan\theta = \frac34$, $\sec\theta = \frac54$, $\cot\theta = \frac43$.
Pythagorean triples make this instant: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25.

### The standard-angle table (learn this cold)
Trick for sine: write $\frac{\sqrt0}{2}, \frac{\sqrt1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt2}{2}, \frac{\sqrt3}{2}, \frac{\sqrt4}{2}$ under $0^\circ, 30^\circ, 45^\circ, 60^\circ, 90^\circ$. Cosine is the same row **backwards**. Tan = sin ÷ cos.

| $\theta$ | $0^\circ$ | $30^\circ$ | $45^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $90^\circ$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sin\theta$ | $0$ | $\frac12$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $1$ |
| $\cos\theta$ | $1$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ | $\frac12$ | $0$ |
| $\tan\theta$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ | $1$ | $\sqrt3$ | not defined |

Reciprocals: $\csc 30^\circ = 2$, $\sec 60^\circ = 2$, $\sec 45^\circ = \sqrt2$, $\cot 60^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$, etc.

### Complementary angles
$\sin(90^\circ - \theta) = \cos\theta$, $\cos(90^\circ - \theta) = \sin\theta$, $\tan(90^\circ - \theta) = \cot\theta$. So $\sin 30^\circ = \cos 60^\circ$, and $\tan 20^\circ\tan 70^\circ = \tan20^\circ\cot20^\circ = 1$.

**Mini example.** $\sin60^\circ\cos30^\circ + \cos60^\circ\sin30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac12\cdot\frac12 = \frac34 + \frac14 = 1$.

> **Recognise it in the exam:** "if $\sin\theta = \frac{3}{5}$ find …", "value of $\sin^2 30^\circ + \cos^2 60^\circ$", "$\tan 1^\circ\tan 2^\circ\cdots\tan 89^\circ$". Tools: the table, Pythagoras, complementary pairs.

lessons.title: 3. Any angle: the unit circle, ASTC and allied angles
lessons.body:
### The unit-circle picture (in words)
Imagine a circle of radius 1 centred at the origin. Start at the point $(1, 0)$ on the positive x-axis and walk anticlockwise around the circle through an angle $\theta$. The point you reach has coordinates
$$(\cos\theta,\ \sin\theta)$$
So **cos is the x-coordinate** (left/right) and **sin is the y-coordinate** (up/down). This works for every angle — obtuse, reflex, negative, or more than a full turn.

| Angle | Point reached | $\cos$ | $\sin$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $0^\circ$ | $(1, 0)$ | $1$ | $0$ |
| $90^\circ$ | $(0, 1)$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| $180^\circ$ | $(-1, 0)$ | $-1$ | $0$ |
| $270^\circ$ | $(0, -1)$ | $0$ | $-1$ |
| $360^\circ$ | back to $(1, 0)$ | $1$ | $0$ |

Since the point never leaves a circle of radius 1: $-1 \le \sin\theta \le 1$ and $-1 \le \cos\theta \le 1$.

### Signs: ASTC ("All Students Take Coffee")
The quadrant decides whether x and y are positive or negative:

| Quadrant | Angles | Positive ratios |
|---|---|---|
| I | $0^\circ$–$90^\circ$ | **A**ll |
| II | $90^\circ$–$180^\circ$ | **S**in (and cosec) |
| III | $180^\circ$–$270^\circ$ | **T**an (and cot) |
| IV | $270^\circ$–$360^\circ$ | **C**os (and sec) |

### Big and negative angles
- Adding a full turn changes nothing: $\sin(\theta + 360^\circ) = \sin\theta$, same for cos. So **subtract multiples of $360^\circ$** first. ($\tan$ even repeats every $180^\circ$.)
- Negative angle = clockwise turn: $\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta$, $\ \sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta$, $\ \tan(-\theta) = -\tan\theta$.

### The reference-angle method (works every time)
1. Reduce the angle to between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$.
2. Find its quadrant.
3. Find the **reference angle** — the acute angle to the x-axis: QII: $180^\circ - \theta$; QIII: $\theta - 180^\circ$; QIV: $360^\circ - \theta$.
4. Value = (same ratio of the reference angle) with the sign from ASTC.

**Mini examples.**
- $\cos 510^\circ$: $510 - 360 = 150^\circ$, QII, reference $30^\circ$, cos is negative in QII → $-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
- $\sin 300^\circ$: QIV, reference $60^\circ$, sin negative → $-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
- $\tan 225^\circ$: QIII, reference $45^\circ$, tan positive → $1$.
- $\cos(-690^\circ) = \cos 690^\circ = \cos 330^\circ$: QIV, reference $30^\circ$, cos positive → $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

### Allied-angle formulas (same thing, written as rules)
- $\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin\theta$, $\ \cos(180^\circ - \theta) = -\cos\theta$
- $\sin(180^\circ + \theta) = -\sin\theta$, $\ \cos(180^\circ + \theta) = -\cos\theta$, $\ \tan(180^\circ + \theta) = \tan\theta$
- $\sin(360^\circ - \theta) = -\sin\theta$, $\ \cos(360^\circ - \theta) = \cos\theta$
- $\sin(90^\circ + \theta) = \cos\theta$, $\ \cos(90^\circ + \theta) = -\sin\theta$

Rule behind them: with $90^\circ$ or $270^\circ$ the function **switches** (sin ↔ cos, tan ↔ cot); with $180^\circ$ or $360^\circ$ it **stays**; the sign always comes from the quadrant of the original angle. In radians, $180^\circ = \pi$: $\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x$, $\cos(\pi + x) = -\cos x$, …

> **Recognise it in the exam:** any angle above $90^\circ$ or negative: "$\cos 480^\circ$", "$\sin(-1110^\circ)$", "$\tan\frac{7\pi}{4}$", "if $\theta$ lies in the second quadrant". Tools: subtract $360^\circ$, reference angle, ASTC.

lessons.title: 4. Identities, compound angles and max/min values
lessons.body:
### Pythagorean identities
On the unit circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, and $x = \cos\theta$, $y = \sin\theta$, so
$$\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$$
Divide by $\cos^2\theta$: $\ 1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$. Divide by $\sin^2\theta$: $\ 1 + \cot^2\theta = \csc^2\theta$.

Uses:
- Simplifying: $(1 - \sin^2\theta)\sec^2\theta = \cos^2\theta\cdot\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta} = 1$.
- $\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1$ factorises as $(\sec\theta - \tan\theta)(\sec\theta + \tan\theta) = 1$, so if $\sec\theta + \tan\theta = k$ then $\sec\theta - \tan\theta = \frac1k$.
- MCQ trick: when an identity question has options, put $\theta = 45^\circ$ (or $30^\circ$) into the question and the options, and match.

### Compound-angle formulas
$$\sin(A \pm B) = \sin A\cos B \pm \cos A\sin B$$
$$\cos(A \pm B) = \cos A\cos B \mp \sin A\sin B \quad(\text{note the sign flips})$$
$$\tan(A \pm B) = \frac{\tan A \pm \tan B}{1 \mp \tan A\tan B}$$
They give values of "non-table" angles:
- $\sin 75^\circ = \sin(45^\circ + 30^\circ) = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac12 = \dfrac{\sqrt3 + 1}{2\sqrt2} = \dfrac{\sqrt6 + \sqrt2}{4}$ $(= \cos 15^\circ)$
- $\sin 15^\circ = \cos 75^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt6 - \sqrt2}{4}$
- $\tan 15^\circ = 2 - \sqrt3$, $\ \tan 75^\circ = 2 + \sqrt3$
- $\tan(45^\circ + \theta) = \dfrac{1 + \tan\theta}{1 - \tan\theta}$

Warning: $\sin(A + B) \ne \sin A + \sin B$. Check: $\sin 90^\circ = 1$ but $\sin 45^\circ + \sin 45^\circ = \sqrt2$.

### Maximum and minimum values
Because the unit-circle point stays on the circle, $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ never go beyond $\pm1$:
- $3 + 2\sin\theta$ ranges from $3 - 2 = 1$ to $3 + 2 = 5$.
- $\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac12\sin2\theta$ has maximum $\frac12$.

The key result: $a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta$ can be rewritten as $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\,\sin(\theta + \alpha)$, so
$$-\sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \ \le\ a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta \ \le\ \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$$
**Mini example.** $6\sin\theta + 8\cos\theta$: $\sqrt{36 + 64} = 10$, so max 10, min $-10$. For $6\sin\theta + 8\cos\theta - 1$: max 9, min $-11$.
The answer is **not** $a + b$ (that would need $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ both equal to 1 at the same time, which never happens).

> **Recognise it in the exam:** "prove/simplify", "if $\sec\theta + \tan\theta = \dots$", "value of $\sin 75^\circ$ / $\tan 15^\circ$", "maximum value of $a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta$". Tools: $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$, the compound formulas, $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.

lessons.title: 5. Double, triple angles and sum-to-product
lessons.body:
### Double angle (put $B = A$ in the compound formulas)
$$\sin 2A = 2\sin A\cos A = \frac{2\tan A}{1 + \tan^2 A}$$
$$\cos 2A = \cos^2 A - \sin^2 A = 2\cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 A = \frac{1 - \tan^2 A}{1 + \tan^2 A}$$
$$\tan 2A = \frac{2\tan A}{1 - \tan^2 A}$$
Rearranged (very common): $1 + \cos 2A = 2\cos^2 A$ and $1 - \cos 2A = 2\sin^2 A$.

**Mini examples.**
- $\sin 15^\circ\cos 15^\circ = \frac12(2\sin15^\circ\cos15^\circ) = \frac12\sin30^\circ = \frac14$.
- $\cos^2 22.5^\circ - \sin^2 22.5^\circ = \cos 45^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$.
- $\dfrac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{\sin 2\theta} = \dfrac{2\sin^2\theta}{2\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \tan\theta$.

### Triple angle
$$\sin 3A = 3\sin A - 4\sin^3 A \qquad \cos 3A = 4\cos^3 A - 3\cos A$$
Spot them in disguise: $3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta$ is just $\sin 3\theta$, so its maximum is 1.

### Product → sum
- $2\sin A\cos B = \sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B)$
- $2\cos A\sin B = \sin(A + B) - \sin(A - B)$
- $2\cos A\cos B = \cos(A + B) + \cos(A - B)$
- $2\sin A\sin B = \cos(A - B) - \cos(A + B)$

### Sum → product
$$\sin C + \sin D = 2\sin\frac{C + D}{2}\cos\frac{C - D}{2} \qquad \sin C - \sin D = 2\cos\frac{C + D}{2}\sin\frac{C - D}{2}$$
$$\cos C + \cos D = 2\cos\frac{C + D}{2}\cos\frac{C - D}{2} \qquad \cos C - \cos D = -2\sin\frac{C + D}{2}\sin\frac{C - D}{2}$$
**Mini example.** $\sin 75^\circ + \sin 15^\circ = 2\sin 45^\circ\cos 30^\circ = 2\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} = \frac{\sqrt6}{2}$.

### Two famous products
$\cos A\cos(60^\circ - A)\cos(60^\circ + A) = \frac14\cos 3A$ and $\sin A\sin(60^\circ - A)\sin(60^\circ + A) = \frac14\sin 3A$.
So $\cos 20^\circ\cos 40^\circ\cos 80^\circ = \frac14\cos 60^\circ = \frac18$.

> **Recognise it in the exam:** "$\sin x\cos x$", "$\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x$", "$\frac{1 - \cos 2x}{\sin 2x}$", a sum like "$\sin 75^\circ + \sin 15^\circ$", a product like "$\cos 20^\circ\cos 40^\circ\cos 80^\circ$". Tools: spot $2A$ or $3A$ hiding inside, then use the table.

lessons.title: 6. Trigonometric equations
lessons.body:
### Why there are infinitely many answers
$\sin\theta = \frac12$ is true at $30^\circ$ and $150^\circ$, and again every full turn later: $390^\circ, 510^\circ, \dots$ and also at $-210^\circ, \dots$. A **general solution** is one formula, with an integer $n$ ($n = 0, \pm1, \pm2, \dots$), that lists all of them. **Principal solutions** are the ones between $0$ and $2\pi$.

### The general-solution table

| Equation | General solution |
|---|---|
| $\sin\theta = 0$ | $\theta = n\pi$ |
| $\cos\theta = 0$ | $\theta = (2n + 1)\frac{\pi}{2}$ |
| $\tan\theta = 0$ | $\theta = n\pi$ |
| $\sin\theta = \sin\alpha$ | $\theta = n\pi + (-1)^n\alpha$ |
| $\cos\theta = \cos\alpha$ | $\theta = 2n\pi \pm \alpha$ |
| $\tan\theta = \tan\alpha$ | $\theta = n\pi + \alpha$ |
| $\sin^2\theta = \sin^2\alpha$ (or $\cos^2$, $\tan^2$) | $\theta = n\pi \pm \alpha$ |

Why cos has "$\pm$": cos is the x-coordinate, and the angles $\alpha$ and $-\alpha$ are mirror images above/below the x-axis, with the same x.

### Method
1. Rearrange to a single "ratio = number".
2. Write the number as the same ratio of a standard angle $\alpha$ (for a negative value: $\sin$/$\tan$ use $-\alpha$; $\cos$ uses $\pi - \alpha$).
3. Apply the formula.

**Mini examples.**
- $2\cos\theta = 1$ → $\cos\theta = \frac12 = \cos\frac{\pi}{3}$ → $\theta = 2n\pi \pm \frac{\pi}{3}$.
- $\tan\theta = -1 = \tan\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ → $\theta = n\pi - \frac{\pi}{4}$. Principal solutions: $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ and $\frac{7\pi}{4}$.
- $2\sin^2\theta - 3\sin\theta + 1 = 0$ factorises as $(2\sin\theta - 1)(\sin\theta - 1) = 0$, so $\sin\theta = \frac12$ or $\sin\theta = 1$.

### Never divide by something that can be zero
In $\sin 2x = \cos x$, write $2\sin x\cos x - \cos x = 0$ → $\cos x(2\sin x - 1) = 0$. Dividing by $\cos x$ instead would lose the solutions $x = \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}$.

### Counting solutions in an interval
List them from the unit circle: $\sin x = \frac12$ in $[0, 2\pi]$ gives $\frac{\pi}{6}$ and $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ — two solutions. A value strictly between $-1$ and $1$ gives **2** solutions per full turn for sin or cos; $\pm 1$ gives only 1.

> **Recognise it in the exam:** "general solution of", "principal solutions", "number of solutions in $[0, 2\pi]$". Tools: the table, factorising, sign rules for negative values.

lessons.title: 7. Inverse trigonometric functions
lessons.body:
### What $\sin^{-1}x$ means
$\sin^{-1}x$ (also written $\arcsin x$) is **"the angle whose sine is $x$"**. It is **not** $\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$.
Many angles have sine $\frac12$ ($30^\circ, 150^\circ, 390^\circ, \dots$), so each inverse function agrees to give one standard answer from a fixed range — the **principal value**.

### Principal-value ranges (the whole chapter hangs on this table)

| Function | Allowed $x$ | Principal value lies in |
|---|---|---|
| $\sin^{-1}x$ | $-1 \le x \le 1$ | $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ |
| $\cos^{-1}x$ | $-1 \le x \le 1$ | $[0, \pi]$ |
| $\tan^{-1}x$ | all real $x$ | $\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ |
| $\cot^{-1}x$ | all real $x$ | $(0, \pi)$ |
| $\sec^{-1}x$ | $x \le -1$ or $x \ge 1$ | $[0, \pi]$, not $\frac{\pi}{2}$ |
| $\csc^{-1}x$ | $x \le -1$ or $x \ge 1$ | $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$, not $0$ |

Picture: $\sin^{-1}$, $\tan^{-1}$, $\csc^{-1}$ answer on the **right half** of the unit circle (quadrants I and IV); $\cos^{-1}$, $\cot^{-1}$, $\sec^{-1}$ answer on the **upper half** (quadrants I and II) and are **never negative**.

### Negative inputs
- $\sin^{-1}(-x) = -\sin^{-1}x$, $\ \tan^{-1}(-x) = -\tan^{-1}x$, $\ \csc^{-1}(-x) = -\csc^{-1}x$
- $\cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1}x$, $\ \cot^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cot^{-1}x$, $\ \sec^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \sec^{-1}x$

**Mini examples.** $\sin^{-1}\left(-\frac12\right) = -\frac{\pi}{6}$. $\ \cos^{-1}\left(-\frac12\right) = \pi - \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{2\pi}{3}$. $\ \tan^{-1}(-1) = -\frac{\pi}{4}$.

### Key identities
- $\sin^{-1}x + \cos^{-1}x = \frac{\pi}{2}$, $\ \tan^{-1}x + \cot^{-1}x = \frac{\pi}{2}$, $\ \sec^{-1}x + \csc^{-1}x = \frac{\pi}{2}$
- $\sin^{-1}\frac1x = \csc^{-1}x$, $\ \cos^{-1}\frac1x = \sec^{-1}x$, $\ \tan^{-1}\frac1x = \cot^{-1}x$ (for $x > 0$)
- $\tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}y = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x + y}{1 - xy}$ (when $xy < 1$); $\ \tan^{-1}x - \tan^{-1}y = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x - y}{1 + xy}$ (when $xy > -1$)
- $2\tan^{-1}x = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1 - x^2}$ for $-1 < x < 1$

**Mini example.** $\tan^{-1}\frac12 + \tan^{-1}\frac13 = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{\frac12 + \frac13}{1 - \frac16} = \tan^{-1}1 = \frac{\pi}{4}$.

### "Inverse of a ratio" traps
- $\sin(\sin^{-1}x) = x$ always (for allowed $x$).
- $\sin^{-1}(\sin\theta) = \theta$ **only if $\theta$ is already in** $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$. Otherwise find the angle in the range with the same sine: $\sin^{-1}\left(\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{\pi}{3}$ (because $\sin\frac{2\pi}{3} = \sin\frac{\pi}{3}$). Similarly $\cos^{-1}\left(\cos\frac{7\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{5\pi}{6}$.
- Mixed expressions use a triangle: $\sin\left(\cos^{-1}\frac35\right)$: angle with $B = 3$, $H = 5$, so $P = 4$ → $\frac45$.

> **Recognise it in the exam:** "principal value of", "$\sin^{-1}$", "$\tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}y$", "$\sin(\cos^{-1}x)$". Tools: the range table first, then the negative-input rules.

lessons.title: 8. Properties of triangles: sine rule, cosine rule, area
lessons.body:
### Notation
In triangle $ABC$ the angles are $A, B, C$ and the side **opposite** each angle is the matching small letter: $a$ faces $A$, $b$ faces $B$, $c$ faces $C$.
- $A + B + C = 180^\circ$
- The **largest side faces the largest angle**; the smallest side faces the smallest angle.

### Sine rule
$$\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C} = 2R$$
($R$ = radius of the circumscribed circle.) Use it when you know **two angles and a side**, or when a question gives a ratio of angles and asks for a ratio of sides: $a : b : c = \sin A : \sin B : \sin C$.
**Mini example.** Angles in ratio $1 : 2 : 3$ → $30^\circ, 60^\circ, 90^\circ$ → sides $\frac12 : \frac{\sqrt3}{2} : 1 = 1 : \sqrt3 : 2$.

### Cosine rule
$$a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \cos A = \frac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}$$
(and similarly for $B$ and $C$). Use it when you know **all three sides**, or two sides and the angle between them.
Quick test on the largest angle: numerator $> 0$ → acute; $= 0$ → right angle; $< 0$ → obtuse.

**Mini example.** Sides 7, 8, 13. The largest side is 13. The angle opposite it:
$$\cos\theta = \frac{7^2 + 8^2 - 13^2}{2\cdot7\cdot8} = \frac{49 + 64 - 169}{112} = \frac{-56}{112} = -\frac12 \Rightarrow \theta = 120^\circ$$
The numerator is negative, so the angle is obtuse — as the quick test says.

### Area of a triangle
$$\Delta = \frac12 bc\sin A = \frac12 ca\sin B = \frac12 ab\sin C$$
("half the product of two sides times the sine of the angle **between** them"). Also Heron's formula $\Delta = \sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}$ with $s = \frac{a + b + c}{2}$, and $\Delta = \dfrac{abc}{4R}$.
**Mini example.** Sides 5 and 8 with $60^\circ$ between them: $\Delta = \frac12\cdot5\cdot8\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} = 10\sqrt3$.

### Projection formula (occasionally asked)
$a = b\cos C + c\cos B$ (and cyclic).

> **Recognise it in the exam:** "in a triangle $ABC$ …", "sides are … find the largest angle", "angles are in the ratio …", "area of triangle with two sides and included angle". Tools: sine rule for angle-heavy data, cosine rule for side-heavy data.

lessons.title: 9. Heights and distances
lessons.body:
### Two angles you must picture
- **Angle of elevation**: you look **up** at something; the angle between your horizontal line of sight and the line to the object.
- **Angle of depression**: you look **down** from a height; the angle between the horizontal and the line down to the object.
Because the two horizontals are parallel, the angle of depression from $P$ to $Q$ **equals** the angle of elevation from $Q$ to $P$.

### The method
1. Draw a right-angled triangle: vertical height, horizontal ground, and the line of sight as the hypotenuse.
2. Mark the known angle at the observer.
3. Almost always use $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{horizontal distance}}$. Use $\sin$ or $\cos$ only if a slanting length (ladder, kite string, wire) is given or asked.

Values you need: $\tan 30^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$, $\tan 45^\circ = 1$, $\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt3$; $\sqrt3 \approx 1.732$.

**Mini example 1 (ladder).** A 10 m ladder makes $60^\circ$ with the ground. Height reached $= 10\sin60^\circ = 5\sqrt3$ m.

**Mini example 2 (IPO 2022).** Two poles of heights 13 m and 7 m stand 8 m apart. Distance between their tops? Join the tops: horizontal gap 8 m, vertical gap $13 - 7 = 6$ m, so distance $= \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = 10$ m. (No trig needed — just Pythagoras.)

**Mini example 3 (shadow).** When the sun's elevation is $45^\circ$, a pole's shadow equals its height. At $60^\circ$ the shadow is $\frac{h}{\sqrt3}$ (shorter); at $30^\circ$ it is $h\sqrt3$ (longer).

### Two observations of the same tower
From two points on the same side, $d$ metres apart, the elevations are $\alpha$ (far) and $\beta$ (near). With $x$ = distance from the near point:
$$h = x\tan\beta = (x + d)\tan\alpha$$
Solve for $x$, then $h$. Special case worth memorising: **$30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$** → the near distance is $x = \frac{d}{2}$ and $h = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}d$.

### Tower seen from a cliff
From the top of a cliff of height $H$, depressions of the top and foot of a tower are $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Horizontal distance $x = \dfrac{H}{\tan\beta}$; the drop from the cliff top to the tower top is $x\tan\alpha$; tower height $= H - x\tan\alpha$.

> **Recognise it in the exam:** "angle of elevation/depression", "shadow", "ladder", "tower", "two poles … distance between their tops". Tools: draw first, $\tan$ = height / distance, Pythagoras for slant distances.

formulas.name: Standard sine values
formulas.when: Cosine is the same list reversed.

formulas.name: Allied angles
formulas.when: 90°/270° switch the function; 180°/360° keep it; sign from ASTC.

formulas.name: Double angle (sin, tan)
formulas.tex: \sin 2A = 2\sin A\cos A = \frac{2\tan A}{1 + \tan^2 A},\quad \tan 2A = \frac{2\tan A}{1 - \tan^2 A}

formulas.name: Product to sum
formulas.tex: 2\sin A\cos B = \sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B),\ 2\cos A\cos B = \cos(A + B) + \cos(A - B)

formulas.name: Sum to product (cos)
formulas.tex: \cos C + \cos D = 2\cos\frac{C + D}{2}\cos\frac{C - D}{2},\ \cos C - \cos D = -2\sin\frac{C + D}{2}\sin\frac{C - D}{2}

examples.solution:
Step 1: Remove full turns: $480^\circ - 360^\circ = 120^\circ$, so $\cos 480^\circ = \cos 120^\circ$.
Step 2: $120^\circ$ is in quadrant II, where only sin is positive → cos is negative.
Step 3: Reference angle $= 180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ$, and $\cos 60^\circ = \frac12$.
Step 4: $\cos 480^\circ = -\frac12$.
Answer: $-\dfrac12$

examples.q: If $\cos\theta = -\dfrac35$ and $\theta$ lies in the third quadrant, find $\sin\theta$ and $\tan\theta$.
examples.solution:
Step 1: Ignore the sign and use a triangle: $B = 3$, $H = 5$, so $P = \sqrt{25 - 9} = 4$.
Step 2: Sizes: $\sin\theta = \frac45$, $\tan\theta = \frac43$ (before signs).
Step 3: In quadrant III only tan (and cot) is positive.
Step 4: $\sin\theta = -\frac45$, $\tan\theta = +\frac43$.
Answer: $\sin\theta = -\dfrac45$, $\tan\theta = \dfrac43$
examples.shortcut: Find the size from the 3-4-5 triangle, then attach the ASTC sign last.

examples.solution:
Step 1: $15^\circ = 45^\circ - 30^\circ$.
Step 2: $\tan(A - B) = \dfrac{\tan A - \tan B}{1 + \tan A\tan B} = \dfrac{1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt3}}{1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt3}} = \dfrac{\sqrt3 - 1}{\sqrt3 + 1}$.
Step 3: Multiply top and bottom by $\sqrt3 - 1$: $\dfrac{(\sqrt3 - 1)^2}{3 - 1} = \dfrac{4 - 2\sqrt3}{2}$.
Step 4: $= 2 - \sqrt3$.
Answer: $2 - \sqrt3$

examples.q: Find the maximum and minimum values of $3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta + 2$.
examples.solution:
Step 1: $a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta$ lies between $-\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ and $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
Step 2: $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$, so $3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta$ lies between $-5$ and $5$.
Step 3: Add 2: maximum $5 + 2 = 7$, minimum $-5 + 2 = -3$.
Answer: max $7$, min $-3$

examples.q: Find the general solution and the principal solutions of $\tan x = -\sqrt3$.
examples.solution:
Step 1: $\tan\frac{\pi}{3} = \sqrt3$, so $-\sqrt3 = \tan\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)$.
Step 2: $\tan x = \tan\alpha \Rightarrow x = n\pi + \alpha$, so $x = n\pi - \frac{\pi}{3}$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$.
Step 3: Principal solutions (in $[0, 2\pi)$): $n = 1$ gives $\frac{2\pi}{3}$; $n = 2$ gives $\frac{5\pi}{3}$.
Answer: $x = n\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3}$; principal solutions $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$
examples.shortcut: tan is negative in quadrants II and IV; reference angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$ → $\pi - \frac{\pi}{3}$ and $2\pi - \frac{\pi}{3}$.
Negative input: $\cos^{-1}$ reflects to $\pi - (\ )$; $\sin^{-1}$ and $\tan^{-1}$ just take the minus outside.

examples.q: The three sides of a triangle are $a$, $\sqrt3a$ and $\sqrt2a$. Find the angle opposite the largest side. (IPO 2022)
examples.solution:
Step 1: Largest side: $\sqrt3 a \approx 1.73a$ (bigger than $\sqrt2 a \approx 1.41a$ and $a$).
Step 2: Cosine rule for the angle $\theta$ opposite it: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{a^2 + (\sqrt2a)^2 - (\sqrt3a)^2}{2\cdot a\cdot\sqrt2a}$.
Step 3: Numerator: $a^2 + 2a^2 - 3a^2 = 0$.
Step 4: $\cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \theta = 90^\circ$.
Answer: $90^\circ$
examples.shortcut: Square the sides: $1, 3, 2$ (times $a^2$). Since $1 + 2 = 3$, Pythagoras holds → right angle.

examples.q: From a point on the ground the angle of elevation of the top of a tower is $30^\circ$. On walking 40 m towards the tower, the angle becomes $60^\circ$. Find the height of the tower.
examples.solution:
Step 1: Let the height be $h$ and the distance from the nearer point be $x$.
Step 2: Near point: $\tan60^\circ = \dfrac{h}{x} \Rightarrow h = \sqrt3x$.
Step 3: Far point: $\tan30^\circ = \dfrac{h}{x + 40} \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{x + 40}{\sqrt3}$.
Step 4: Equate: $\sqrt3x = \dfrac{x + 40}{\sqrt3} \Rightarrow 3x = x + 40 \Rightarrow x = 20$.
Step 5: $h = 20\sqrt3$ m $\approx 34.6$ m.
Answer: $20\sqrt3$ m
examples.shortcut: For elevations $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ with a walk of $d$: $h = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}d = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\times40 = 20\sqrt3$.

traps: Mixing degrees and radians: $\pi$ means $180^\circ$ only inside an angle. Arc length $l = r\theta$ needs $\theta$ in radians — using $60$ instead of $\frac{\pi}{3}$ gives a wildly wrong answer.
Switching the function with $180^\circ$ or $360^\circ$. Only $90^\circ$ and $270^\circ$ switch sin ↔ cos; $\cos(180^\circ - \theta) = -\cos\theta$, not $\sin\theta$.
Taking the sign from the reference angle instead of the original quadrant. $\cos 120^\circ$ is negative because $120^\circ$ is in quadrant II, even though $\cos 60^\circ$ is positive.
Treating $\sin(A + B)$ as $\sin A + \sin B$, or $\sin 2A$ as $2\sin A$. Use the compound/double-angle formulas.
Writing the maximum of $a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta$ as $a + b$. It is $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ ($3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta$ has max 5, not 7).
Using $n\pi + (-1)^n\alpha$ for cosine equations. For $\cos\theta = \cos\alpha$ the general solution is $2n\pi \pm \alpha$.

Giving $\cos^{-1}\left(-\frac12\right) = -\frac{\pi}{3}$. $\cos^{-1}$ is never negative: it is $\pi - \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{2\pi}{3}$. Likewise $\sin^{-1}(\sin\theta) = \theta$ only when $\theta \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$.
In heights and distances, using $\sin$ when the horizontal distance is given (use $\tan$), or dividing by $\cos x$ in an equation and losing the solutions where $\cos x = 0$.

practice.explanation:
$480^\circ - 360^\circ = 120^\circ$, so $\sin480^\circ = \sin120^\circ$.
$120^\circ$ is in quadrant II, where sin is positive.
Reference angle $180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ$: $\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
Answer: (c) $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$

$315^\circ$ is in quadrant IV, where only cos (and sec) is positive → tan is negative.
Reference angle $360^\circ - 315^\circ = 45^\circ$: $\tan45^\circ = 1$.
$\tan315^\circ = -1$.
Answer: (a) $-1$

practice.q: The angle $\dfrac{7\pi}{4}$ radians, in degrees, is
practice.explanation:
Replace $\pi$ by $180^\circ$.
$\dfrac{7\times180^\circ}{4} = 7\times45^\circ = 315^\circ$.
Answer: (d) $315^\circ$

$300^\circ = 360^\circ - 60^\circ$ → quadrant IV, where cos (and sec) is positive.
$\cos300^\circ = \cos 60^\circ = \dfrac12$.
$\sec300^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\cos300^\circ} = 2$.
Answer: (c) $2$

$\sin30^\circ = \frac12 \Rightarrow \sin^2 30^\circ = \frac14$.
$\cos60^\circ = \frac12 \Rightarrow \cos^2 60^\circ = \frac14$.
$\tan45^\circ = 1 \Rightarrow \tan^2 45^\circ = 1$.
Sum $= \frac14 + \frac14 + 1 = \frac32$.
Answer: (a) $\dfrac32$

practice.q: An arc of a circle of radius 21 cm subtends an angle of $60^\circ$ at the centre. Its length is (take $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$)
practice.explanation:
Convert to radians: $60^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
$l = r\theta = 21\times\dfrac{\pi}{3} = 7\pi$.
$7\times\dfrac{22}{7} = 22$ cm.
Answer: (b) $22$ cm
Shortcut: 1260 cm is what you get by multiplying $21\times60$ without converting to radians.

practice.q: If $\cos\theta = \dfrac{8}{17}$ and $\theta$ is acute, then $\tan\theta$ equals
practice.explanation:
$\cos\theta = \dfrac{B}{H}$: $B = 8$, $H = 17$.
$P = \sqrt{17^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{289 - 64} = \sqrt{225} = 15$.
$\tan\theta = \dfrac{P}{B} = \dfrac{15}{8}$.
($\frac{8}{15}$ is $\cot\theta$; $\frac{15}{17}$ is $\sin\theta$.)
Answer: (a) $\dfrac{15}{8}$

$\sin^{-1}(-x) = -\sin^{-1}x$.
$\sin^{-1}\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
So the value is $-\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, which lies in $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$.
($\frac{4\pi}{3}$ and $\frac{5\pi}{3}$ also have sine $-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ but are outside the principal range.)
Answer: (c) $-\dfrac{\pi}{3}$

$\cos^{-1}(-x) = \pi - \cos^{-1}x$.
$\cos^{-1}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
Value $= \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ (inside $[0, \pi]$).
Answer: (a) $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$

Maximum of $a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta$ is $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
$\sqrt{25 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = 13$.
Answer: (d) $13$
Shortcut: 5-12-13 triple. 17 ($= 5 + 12$) is the trap.

$105^\circ = 60^\circ + 45^\circ$.
$\cos(A + B) = \cos A\cos B - \sin A\sin B = \dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} - \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$.
$= \dfrac{1 - \sqrt3}{2\sqrt2} = \dfrac{\sqrt2 - \sqrt6}{4}$ (multiply top and bottom by $\sqrt2$).
Answer: (b) $\dfrac{\sqrt2 - \sqrt6}{4}$
Shortcut: $105^\circ$ is in quadrant II, so cos is negative — only (b) and (d) are negative; $\cos105^\circ = -\sin15^\circ \approx -0.26$ is small, so (b).

$\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta$, so we need $\cos1110^\circ$.
$1110^\circ - 3\times360^\circ = 1110^\circ - 1080^\circ = 30^\circ$.
$\cos30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
Answer: (d) $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$

practice.q: If $\tan A = \dfrac56$ and $\tan B = \dfrac{1}{11}$, where $A$ and $B$ are acute, then $A + B$ equals
practice.explanation:
$\tan(A + B) = \dfrac{\tan A + \tan B}{1 - \tan A\tan B}$.
Top: $\dfrac56 + \dfrac{1}{11} = \dfrac{55 + 6}{66} = \dfrac{61}{66}$. Bottom: $1 - \dfrac{5}{66} = \dfrac{61}{66}$.
$\tan(A + B) = 1$, and $A + B$ is between $0$ and $\pi$, so $A + B = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
Answer: (a) $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$

$\sin A\cos A = \dfrac12(2\sin A\cos A) = \dfrac12\sin2A$.
$= \dfrac12\sin45^\circ = \dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}$.
($\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ forgets the $\frac12$.)
Answer: (c) $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}$

Triangle: $P = 5$, $H = 13$, so $B = \sqrt{169 - 25} = 12$.
Size of $\tan\theta = \dfrac{5}{12}$.
$\theta$ is in quadrant II, where tan is negative.
$\tan\theta = -\dfrac{5}{12}$.
Answer: (d) $-\dfrac{5}{12}$

$4\sin\theta - 3\cos\theta$ lies between $-\sqrt{16 + 9} = -5$ and $5$.
Minimum of the whole expression $= 3 + (-5) = -2$.
Answer: (b) $-2$
Shortcut: $-5$ forgets the constant 3; $-4$ uses $4 + 3 = 7$ instead of 5.

Negative value for cos: use $\pi - \alpha$. $\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac12$, so $-\dfrac12 = \cos\left(\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.
$\cos\theta = \cos\alpha \Rightarrow \theta = 2n\pi \pm \alpha$.
$\theta = 2n\pi \pm \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.
(Option (a) is the sine pattern; option (d) ignores the minus sign.)
Answer: (c) $2n\pi \pm \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$

practice.q: In a triangle with sides $a = 3$, $b = 5$, $c = 7$, the largest angle is
practice.explanation:
The largest angle $C$ faces the largest side $c = 7$.
$\cos C = \dfrac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab} = \dfrac{9 + 25 - 49}{2\cdot3\cdot5} = \dfrac{-15}{30} = -\dfrac12$.
$\cos C = -\dfrac12 \Rightarrow C = 120^\circ$.
Answer: (b) $120^\circ$

Sine rule: $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B}$.
$b = \dfrac{a\sin B}{\sin A} = \dfrac{4\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2}}{\frac12} = \dfrac{8}{\sqrt2}$.
$= 4\sqrt2$.
Answer: (d) $4\sqrt2$
Shortcut: $2\sqrt2$ comes from flipping the ratio ($\sin A/\sin B$).

practice.q: The area of a triangle with $b = 6$, $c = 8$ and $A = 30^\circ$ is
practice.explanation:
$\Delta = \frac12 bc\sin A$.
$= \frac12\times6\times8\times\sin30^\circ = 24\times\frac12 = 12$.
Answer: (a) $12$

practice.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point 30 m from its foot is $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is
practice.explanation:
$\tan60^\circ = \dfrac{h}{30}$.
$h = 30\tan60^\circ = 30\sqrt3$ m.
Answer: (d) $30\sqrt3$ m
Shortcut: $10\sqrt3$ comes from using $\tan30^\circ$ by mistake.

practice.q: Two poles of heights 18 m and 13 m stand on level ground 12 m apart. The distance between their tops is
practice.explanation:
Join the tops: the horizontal gap is 12 m.
The vertical gap is $18 - 13 = 5$ m.
Distance $= \sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{144 + 25} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ m.
Answer: (b) $13$ m
Shortcut: 5-12-13 triple. $\sqrt{313}$ wrongly uses the full 13 m instead of the difference.

$4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta = \cos3\theta$ (triple-angle formula).
So the expression is $\cos3\theta + 2$.
The largest value of $\cos3\theta$ is 1, so the maximum is $1 + 2 = 3$.
(9 adds the coefficients $4 + 3 + 2$; 1 forgets the $+2$.)
Answer: (b) $3$

$\tan^{-1}(\tan\theta) = \theta$ only if $\theta$ is in $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$; $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ is not.
$\tan\dfrac{3\pi}{4} = -1$ (quadrant II, tan negative).
$\tan^{-1}(-1) = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, which is in the range.
Answer: (c) $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$

$\tan^{-1}1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac12\right) = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.
$\sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac12\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
Sum $= \dfrac{3\pi}{12} + \dfrac{8\pi}{12} - \dfrac{2\pi}{12} = \dfrac{9\pi}{12} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.
Answer: (c) $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$
Shortcut: $\frac{5\pi}{12}$ and $-\frac{\pi}{4}$ come from taking $\cos^{-1}(-\frac12)$ as $\frac{\pi}{3}$ or $-\frac{\pi}{3}$.

practice.q: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio $1 : 1 : 4$. The corresponding sides are in the ratio
practice.explanation:
$x + x + 4x = 180^\circ \Rightarrow x = 30^\circ$: angles $30^\circ, 30^\circ, 120^\circ$.
Sine rule: $a : b : c = \sin30^\circ : \sin30^\circ : \sin120^\circ$.
$= \dfrac12 : \dfrac12 : \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = 1 : 1 : \sqrt3$.
Answer: (a) $1 : 1 : \sqrt3$
Shortcut: Sides are **not** in the same ratio as angles — use sines.

practice.q: From a point on level ground the angle of elevation of the top of a tower is $30^\circ$. After walking 20 m towards the tower it becomes $45^\circ$. The height of the tower is
practice.explanation:
Let height $h$, distance from the nearer point $x$.
$\tan45^\circ = \dfrac{h}{x} \Rightarrow h = x$.
$\tan30^\circ = \dfrac{h}{x + 20} \Rightarrow \sqrt3h = h + 20$.
$h(\sqrt3 - 1) = 20 \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{20}{\sqrt3 - 1} = \dfrac{20(\sqrt3 + 1)}{3 - 1} = 10(\sqrt3 + 1)$ m $\approx 27.3$ m.
Answer: (d) $10(\sqrt3 + 1)$ m
Shortcut: The $h = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}d$ rule is only for the $30^\circ/60^\circ$ pair — here it would give the trap $10\sqrt3$.

Use $\sin A\sin(60^\circ - A)\sin(60^\circ + A) = \frac14\sin3A$ with $A = 20^\circ$.
$60^\circ - 20^\circ = 40^\circ$ and $60^\circ + 20^\circ = 80^\circ$ — the given product exactly.
Value $= \frac14\sin60^\circ = \frac14\times\frac{\sqrt3}{2} = \frac{\sqrt3}{8}$.
Answer: (a) $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{8}$
Shortcut: $\frac18$ is the answer for the cosine product $\cos20^\circ\cos40^\circ\cos80^\circ$ — do not mix them up.

practice.q: The number of solutions of $\sin2x = \sin x$ in $[0, 2\pi]$ is
practice.explanation:
$2\sin x\cos x - \sin x = 0 \Rightarrow \sin x\,(2\cos x - 1) = 0$.
$\sin x = 0$: $x = 0, \pi, 2\pi$ (both ends are included in $[0, 2\pi]$).
$\cos x = \dfrac12$: $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$.
Total 5 solutions.
Answer: (d) $5$
Shortcut: Dividing both sides by $\sin x$ loses the three roots of $\sin x = 0$ and gives the trap answer 2.

practice.q: From the top of a 60 m high cliff, the angles of depression of the top and the foot of a tower are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is
practice.explanation:
Foot of tower: $\tan60^\circ = \dfrac{60}{x} \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{60}{\sqrt3} = 20\sqrt3$ m (horizontal distance).
Top of tower: the drop from the cliff top is $x\tan30^\circ = 20\sqrt3\times\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} = 20$ m.
Tower height $= 60 - 20 = 40$ m.
Answer: (a) $40$ m
Shortcut: 20 m is the drop, not the tower; $20\sqrt3$ m is the horizontal distance.
